scope: The 1834 box, whole: the forks, the main stem to the fort, the river turned south behind the baymouth spit to its natural outlet at Swearingen's half mile, the lake shore south of the outlet, and the ground south to the box floor at N -3800 - which takes in the Fort-to-Eighteenth-Street corridor the 1812 scene needs. South of Twelfth Street every vertex is conjectural, by the carried evidence_limit; the battle ground is therefore modelled ground and is NOT a reconstruction from evidence, and this spec says so rather than letting the box's extent imply otherwise.
standard: No survey of this ground exists before Wright's of 1834, and no level of it before the 1850s. Every land elevation here is an 1835 dossier zone carried back twenty-three years, every planform line is a reading of 1834 with the works removed, and the lake stage of 1812 is not recorded at all. So nothing in this spec is better than `inferred`, every surface it AUTHORS for 1812 is `reconstructed`, and the generator must emit no land vertex `documented`.

claims.label: lake_stage_1812
notes: No lake stage of 1812 is recorded, and the dossier grades even the 1835 one conjectural (zone 2, 580 +/- 1.5 ft ASL). The water stands at the 1835 plane so the two epochs' ground can be compared and so every carried bank keeps the freeboard its zone gives it; the historic range of 576-582 ft ASL (dossier section 1.2) is the bound, Z -4 to +2. A lower 1812 lake would widen every beach and lower the river against its banks; a higher one would drown the spit, whose chosen crest is +4. Replaced by any stage reconstruction for the 1810s (NOAA/GLERL Michigan-Huron series).

The 1812 water is the plane Z = 0, which generators/terrain_gen_e1830.py writes through terrain_gen.write_heightfield at a literal zero (heightfield.json water_surface_m) rather than reading surface_ft. range_ft is the zone's bound and dossier_zone a record label for the panel; neither is a build input.

transcribes.work: Journal of Lieutenant James Strode Swearingen, kept on the march from Detroit to Chicago in temporary command of the company sent to establish the first Fort Dearborn; entry for Wednesday 17 August 1803, the day of arrival
transcribes.note: Carries the only period measurement of the Chicago river this project has: about 30 yards wide and upwards of 18 feet deep at the fort site, a south bank about 8 feet high half a mile above the mouth, the opposite bank lower by not more than two feet BY APPEARANCES, and the banks above quite low. the height of the south (fort) bank at that point, about 8 feet
that the north bank was lower, by an estimate made by eye and stated as a maximum of two feet
that the river above the fort had quite low banks — the only statement here about the reach this project models

notes: The channel behind the spit, from the fort south to the outlet. The 1834 spec's old_south_channel takes zone 26's middle, -2.5 ft, for a backwater silting into a lagoon after the cut took the river; in 1812 the whole river ran down it, so the DEEP end of zone 26's range is taken, -4 ft. It is not carried down to the main stem's -12 to -18 (zone 20): the bar 'admitted only boats' (dossier section 3.2), the schooner Tracy anchored half a mile out in 1803 for that reason, and Harrison's 1830 plat letters the old mouth 'very shallow'. citations.carries_no_document: Opened and read in full 2026-08-11 (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chicago_River&action=raw, HTTP 200). Looked for a transcription of Swearingen's 1803 journal and there is none: the page paraphrases him in one sentence of its own prose and footnotes the reprinting, which is a citation and not a reprinting. Every other passage this project draws on here is the same shape. So this record's rung is a judgement about an encyclopedia article — later scholarship, tier 4 — and the documents behind it have to be fetched on their own terms. Where it sends you: Quaife 1913, pp. 373-377 for Swearingen; Holland, Chicago in Maps (2005), pp. 102-109 and Andreas vol. 1, pp. 234-235 for the harbour works.

the north bank's height: its '6 ft' is arithmetic on a bounded visual estimate and appears nowhere in the journal

any sourced statement of the river's surface gradient: the sluggish-flow sentence the flat water surface rests on carries no footnote of its own

notes: The 1834 bar's surface carried onto the 1812 spit, at the same +4 ft crest and 12 m face (1:9.8, zone 4's beach slope). Of the five reasons the 1834 spec gives for taking zone 7's LOW end, four hold for 1812 and one does not. Holding: the soldiers of Fort Dearborn trenched this bar with hand tools between 1816 and 1828, so it was low enough to dig through in the years after this scene; the 1839 Fort Dearborn Addition reading of the ground east of Michigan Avenue as 'at best ... a low sandbar'; the direction of the error, because an 8 ft ridge here would hide the river behind a dune it never was; and the dossier's own zone 3 ridge at +9 to +10, which the young end of the same littoral system cannot equal. Not holding: the mid-1830s high-water phase, which is an 1835 fact. The 1812 stage is unknown (lake_stage_1812), so it neither raises nor lowers the choice, and +4 stands on the other four. The planform is Wright's 1834 bar carried whole; over most of its length it is 108-164 m wide, wider than zone 7's 100-300 ft, and that is the trace's reading and is not narrowed here. The surface is emitted CONJECTURAL in the confidence channel: its shape is evidence, its height is not.

feature, crest_ft and face_m are read: generators/terrain_gen_e1830.py lifts the spit and its neck to crest_ft across face_m. range_ft is zone 7's bound and dossier_zone a label. material is not drawn: the ground is one surface colour across the box, as the 1834 surface_materials rows declare, and L362 admits it.

transcribes.note: PRINTED AT LENGTH AND NOT MERELY CITED. At pages 34-35 the volume introduces the Kinzie and Clybourn genealogy as 'best told by Rufus Blanchard ... He says:' and sets the whole passage as a block quotation, which is why bk_mose1_019 - Benjamin Hall's 1830 arrival and the town's first tannery - is a reading of Blanchard through Moses and Kirkland and not of Moses and Kirkland. This project does not hold Blanchard and cannot check the transcription. Blanchard in turn credits Benjamin Hall himself for the detail, so the chain to the fact is three deep and the claim says so.

what_it_supplies: A TRADE CENSUS OF THE WHOLE TOWN, at page 95: the State census taken between 1 September and December 1835 counted 3,297 people, forty-four stores, two book stores, four druggists, two silversmiths and jewellers, two tin and copper manufactories, two printing offices, two breweries, one steam saw-mill, one iron foundry, four storage and forwarding houses, eight taverns, one lottery office, one bank, five churches, seven schools, twenty-two lawyers, fourteen physicians, and a lyceum and reading room. The project had no denominator for its business layer and this is one - for December 1835 and not for July.

A BUILDING WITH FOUR OF THE FIVE FIELDS data/structures/ WANTS, at page 90: John S. C. Hogan's story-and-a-half log storehouse, 45 by 18 feet, at the angle where Lake and South Water streets meet, with the post office partitioned off inside it from 2 November 1832.

TWO RESIDENCES STATED AS SUCH, which is the field the town is thinnest in: Rev. Jeremiah Porter lodging and keeping his study in the second storey of Peck's store from May 1833 (page 571), and John Dean Caton renting the back room and attic of Dr Temple's Temple Building from December 1833, sleeping in the attic and practising law in the back room, and sub-letting desk-room in it to his competitor Spring (page 577).

BUSINESSES GIVEN BY CORNER, LOT OR LANDMARK: Dole's and Peck's first frame business buildings at the south-east corners of South Water and Dearborn and of South Water and La Salle (page 89); Peck's two-storey frame store of black walnut brought from Detroit, occupied in the fall of 1831 (page 570); Sylvester Marsh killing beef under an old elm on the open prairie at what became Monroe Street from the winter of 1833-4 (page 389); William Jones's lots 2 and 7 in block 17 fronting Water and Lake (page 542).

OCCUPATIONS AND ARRIVALS for men this project already holds: Philo Carpenter as the town's first druggist, arriving within a month before 19 August 1832; Benjamin Hall as proprietor of the first tannery ever established there, arriving 1830; Dole, Clybourn, the Noble brothers and Gurdon S. Hubbard beginning the slaughtering and packing trade in 1832; the 1833 spring arrivals including Caton, Kimball and Asahel Pierce; and Hubbard's permanent residence dated to 1832 by the compiler's own reason for leaving him off a list.

TWO PRESENCE LISTS: the twenty-two men who signed the Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company roll on 7 October 1835 (pages 207-208), and, unread and left for its own ticket, the 'LIST OF ACTUAL SETTLERS AT CHICAGO, PRIOR TO 1830' at pages 78-79, about thirty rows with nativity, year and remarks columns.
ONE STATEMENT ABOUT THE GROUND OF THE SCENE, at page 79: the winter of 1834-5 was open, with little snow, front doors standing open all winter, and cattle living on grass on the river bank.
what_it_does_not_supply: MOST OF WHAT IT WAS FETCHED FOR. Of the forty-nine lead surnames the Newberry index flagged against this work, thirteen earned a claim, twenty-one appear only outside the pre-1836 window, eight appear early and say nothing usable, one (`black`) is only ever the adjective, four are unresolved because the volume carries a surname one character from the index card's spelling, and two are absent outright. The full row-by-row result is committed at data/research/books/moses_kirkland_v1_lead_surnames.json so the next run does not pay for the search twice.

VOLUME 2, WHICH IS HALF THE WORK. Only volume 1 is read. The Newberry cards do not say which volume they cite, so an absence recorded here may simply be in the other book, and every ABSENT verdict in the lookup file says so on itself.

AN INDEPENDENT VOICE. It is a compilation of 1895 and it names its own authorities on the pages read: Andreas for Garrett's $1,800,000 of auction sales, Bross's History of Chicago page 38 for the earliest deeds, the Story of Chicago page 130 for Caton's election tally, Hurlbut's Chicago Antiquities pages 37-8 for the pre-1830 settler list, S. R. Beggs's West and Northwest page 95 for the Black Hawk alarm, and Rufus Blanchard's Discovery of the Northwest and History of Chicago (1881) quoted at length for the Kinzie-Clybourn genealogy. Where the sentence itself credits another work, the claim says so and the citation must go to that work and not to this one.
A SINGLE ADDRESS IN THE MODERN SENSE, and no street numbers. Positions here are corners, lots, blocks, a river bank and a tree.

ANY DATE FINER THAN THE YEAR for two things this project wanted finer: Caton's marriage, which is given as '1835' with the scene date sitting in the middle of it, and the Hubbard-Marsh packing partnership, which is 'later'.

CONSISTENCY WITH ITSELF. Page 89 dates Dole's and Peck's first frame business buildings to 1832 while page 570 has Peck's occupied in the fall of 1831; page 207 forms the Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company on 7 October 1835 while page 570 has it organised on 20 October 1835. Both readings of each are recorded and neither is adopted.

notes: T-2066. South of Twelfth Street the 1812 ground was a flat plateau: every row from the beach's back (25 m inland) to 400 m inland read 9.4 ft (2.86 m), the South Division's carried plain, with no hill and no swale. Three readings say otherwise, and two of them are already in data/terrain/1812_evacuation_readings.json § landform, where the route of 15 August 1812 is drawn from them. Moses & Kirkland (1895, pp. 49-50) put 'the low wave-washed and wind-swept sand-hills' beginning at about Twelfth Street, with the shore flat north of it. The same book (p. 60) says 'the shore sand-hills were not high and not continuous', and that 'the surface of the bank, a hundred feet or more back from the water, varied from ten to twenty feet in height above its level'. Quaife (1913, p. 226) has 'a row of sand hills, or ridges, which ran between the prairie and the beach, parallel to the latter and distant from it about one hundred yards'. Dossier zone 5 sizes the fort's sand hills as hummocks 50-150 ft across with +10 to +14 ft peaks; its own source (chicagology_prefire274) is not cited here, because its rights are unresolved and nothing may be built from it (AGENTS.md rule 6), and no figure below rests on it alone. So the forms are built on the north_lake_dunes machinery (generators/terrain_gen.py § the lakefront dunes), measured inland from the lake's edge, row by row. The bank's near face is a ridge centred 40 m (131 ft) back from the water. It stands +5.5 ft on the 9.4 ft plain, so its crests reach 14.9 ft. Quaife's row is a ridge centred at his hundred yards, 91.44 m, the figure the route's attack zone already uses. It stands +9.0 ft, so its crests reach 18.4 ft. Between them, at 64 m, is a swale up to 1.5 ft below the plain: the low wet ground behind a foredune where a sand prairie stands. Hummock noise breaks every ridge into hills 20-40 m across, inside zone 5's 50-150 ft, because the hills were 'not continuous'. Where the noise lets a ridge down, the ground is the plain's own 9.4 ft. That is 0.6 ft under M&K's low figure and inside lake_stage_1812's own -4 to +2 ft uncertainty, so their ten-to-twenty is met by the hills and not forced onto every cell. The beach (the bank face, 25 m) is left as it was, so the column's route on the waterline keeps its ground. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: every position, height and width. The readings fix that the hills existed, where they began, roughly how far back they stood and how high the bank rose, and they place no single hill. THE DISAGREEMENT IS KEPT, NOT RECONCILED: Quaife starts the ridges at the river mouth, 1.6 km north of M&K's Twelfth Street. North of Twelfth the carried 1834 `south_lake_dunes` reach (N -700 to -2120, L334, built on dossier zone 5's 'white sand hills both to the north and south' of the fort) already stands, and this block adds nothing there. The north end therefore fades in over the 60 m south of the evidence_limit line, and the south end runs past the box floor so it does not fade inside the box. Admitted in docs/LIBERTIES.md L392.
